The Rene N4 alloy was developed for gas turbine engine blades and has a nominal composition of 3.7 Al, 4.2 Ti, 4 Ta, 0.5 Nb, 6 W, 1.5 Mo, 9 Cr, 7.5 Co, balance Ni, in weight percent.
The average size and volume fraction of the γ' phase in the Rene N4 alloy were about 0.25μm and 65v/o, respectively.
The [111] specimens, which had the highest Schmid factor for primary cube slip, exhibited cube slip (001)[110] at all temperatures, even room temperature.
The range of orientations exhibiting cube slip expanded with increasing test temperature, until at 980°C only orientations very near the [001] or [011] exhibited octahedral slip.

A tension-compression anisotropy was observed for octahedral slip at 760°C, where the [001] orientation was stronger in tension than in compression, and the [011] orientation showed the opposite behavior.

The Lall, Chin, and Pope (LCP) model provided a better fit for the orientation dependence of yield strengths compared to Schmid's Law, as it accounted for an orientation-dependent tension-compression anisotropy.

The term in the LCP model accounting for the effect of the applied stress on promoting constriction of the dissociated dislocations on the octahedral plane was found to be the most important, while the term representing the effect of the stress on promoting cube cross-slip was relatively unimportant in both Rene N4 and the alloy PWA 1480.

Above 760°C, which is about the peak strength temperature in Rene N4, deviations from Schmid's Law were reduced, and the orientation and tension-compression dependencies of yield strength for octahedral slip changed, with yield strengths being somewhat higher in compression than in tension for the orientations exhibiting octahedral slip.
Both cube and octahedral slip in Rene N4 exhibited a peak in strength near 760°C, suggesting a thermally activated locking mechanism for dislocations on both slip systems.

It was proposed that the observed tension-compression anisotropy for cube slip was due to the resolved stress acting to constrict the partials formed by the dissociation of dislocations on the cube plane, which should aid slip on the cube plane, the opposite of the case for octahedral slip.
